title: What Zen is
hook: Chan in China, Seon in Korea, Thien in Vietnam, Zen in Japan: the school of meditation

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sutras went back on the shelf: a sick layman, a net of jewels, a pointing finger, a stone by the road. Your line: the library, opened. Which image did you keep? Day one thousand two hundred six.

On a scroll in a meditation hall hangs a single character, brushed in black ink. Show it to a monk in China and she reads it Chan. In Korea, a monk reads the same brushstrokes as Seon. In Vietnam, Thien. In Japan, Zen. Four countries, four sounds, and one shape on the paper. The word has slipped into English as a mood: a zen garden, a zen playlist, feeling very zen about the traffic. But on that scroll it names something more particular, a whole school of Buddhism. Today's word: Zen.
screen: `ONE CHARACTER IN BLACK INK.` → `FOUR WAYS TO READ IT.` → `A WHOLE SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Chan, Seon, Thien, Zen: these are not four schools that happen to sound alike. They are one Chinese word, carried into neighboring languages and said with each language's own mouth. Tradition traces the word itself back to the Sanskrit dhyana, meditation. So the school's name is, quite plainly, the meditation school. Second, what that name puts at the center. For the last few weeks this path has been reading sutras, the long shelf of the Mahayana. Zen communities chant sutras too. But the school's name points somewhere else first: to sitting. Not a book on the lap, a body on a cushion. The teaching it points to is the one that happens when someone sits down, settles, and looks directly at their own mind. Third, one practice, many accents. As the meditation school traveled, each land gave it a voice of its own. In the coming weeks this path will meet them: Korea's great question, carried through the day; Vietnam's joining of sitting and chanting; in Japan, a school that works with koans and a school of just sitting. They differ, sometimes, in emphasis. They share the same posture. Fourth, what this means for the next stretch. Before the poems and the famous puzzles, before the old masters and the oxherding pictures, comes the body. So this week starts at the bottom: how to sit, where the hands go, where the eyes rest, what to do with the breath. That's not a warm-up for Zen. As some Zen teachers put it, it is Zen.
screen: `ONE WORD, FOUR MOUTHS.` · `THE MEDITATION SCHOOL.` · `ONE PRACTICE, MANY ACCENTS.` · `FIRST, THE BODY.` · then, large: `CHAN · SEON · THIEN · ZEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: say the four names. Sit comfortably and let the breath come and go. On one out-breath, say quietly, Chan. Let the sound fade. On the next, Seon. Then Thien. Then Zen. Between each name, rest in the quiet it leaves behind. Notice that the names are different and the quiet after them is the same. When you've said all four, let the words go and just sit, the way someone has sat in each of those countries. The bell holds the time.
Zen. The Japanese reading of a word that is Chan in China, Seon in Korea and Thien in Vietnam: the meditation school of Buddhism. Today's word.
Your line: four names, one practice. Today, when you hear the word zen used for a mood or a product, remember the four names, and the sitting underneath them. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: Chan, Seon, Thien and Zen communities in China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan and beyond gather to sit in meditation, usually alongside chanting, ritual and work, and many centers welcome beginners to sit with them.
